title: Handcuffs and Backup Centers
brief: Which backups would step into a big role if the starter ahead of them misses time, and which of them have value on their own? It must explain that in our daily league with 2 bench spots most handcuffs are waiver pickups, not draft stashes.
summary: In our daily 12-team league, a handcuff is only worth a draft pick if he helps you while the starter is healthy and would start for 30-plus minutes if the starter went down. Most backups in our data rank outside the 144 players we draft. Leave them on waivers, keep FAB ready and add them the day the starter gets hurt, instead of using one of our two bench spots on them.

sections.heading: What makes a handcuff worth anything

paragraphs.text: A handcuff in fantasy basketball is not the same as one in fantasy football. He must have value on his own, plus big upside if the starter gets hurt. A backup who only pays off after an injury is not a handcuff we want to draft.

The best case is a clear one-for-one backup who would start and play 30-plus minutes if the starter got hurt. The fewer players ahead of him in the rotation, the fewer injuries it takes to raise his minutes. A deep bench player who needs several teammates hurt is not a must-draft player.

Backup point guards are a common trap. If the team has several ball handlers, wings can take over the role and the backup gains little. Role players with upside can still get a usage spike when a teammate sits, so look at who actually takes the shots and assists. Do not just go by who is listed second at the position.

sections.heading: Why most handcuffs are waiver pickups here

paragraphs.text: We draft 12 players: 10 starters and only 2 bench spots, and we set lineups daily. A backup playing 15 to 20 minutes a night takes up one of those two bench spots and gives you almost nothing until someone gets hurt. Most handcuffs in our data rank well outside the 144 drafted players, so they will still be on waivers when the injury comes. A backup center in particular is not worth rostering until the starter ahead of him is out.

Waivers run on FAB and process daily, with up to 6 adds per week. That means you can react to injury news within a day. Do not pay for a stash at the auction. Save FAB for the week a starter goes down, and bid hard when the backup is a clear one-for-one starter. Upside that depends on other players getting hurt is not something to build a roster around.

The experts do not fully agree. One side says backups one injury away from starting are valid late fliers. They also say a late pick on a teammate who should start can insure your own star, and a strong per-minute backup big is worth drafting. The other side says late upside picks need a realistic path to a role, and that players who only pay off if someone else gets hurt are poor late picks. For us, the second view wins in most cases because of the 2 bench spots. The first view applies only to the last 1 USD of your roster, and only for a backup who already plays real minutes.

sections.heading: Backup centers: stream them, rarely stash them

paragraphs.text: Drafting a backup center and waiting for the starter to be traded is usually a waste. That is even more true if he is not a strong per-minute producer. Leave these players on waivers on draft day.

There is one exception. A backup big with strong per-minute production behind an injury-prone starter can be worth a last pick, because he becomes valuable once the starter misses time. Watch backup center battles behind injury-prone starters in the first weeks, since whoever wins those starts has fantasy value.

Once a backup center starts, he can be an elite streamer. He also picks up extra minutes on nights when the starter is in foul trouble or not scoring. Prefer a backup big who can play back-to-backs over an injury-limited one, because his minutes are steadier. In practice, use one of your 6 weekly adds on him for his spot starts, then drop him when the starter returns.

At the auction on 2026-10-18, only buy a backup who helps a build already, and only with your final 1 to 3 USD. If you own a star, a late pick on a teammate who should start is fair insurance. A pure backup with no standalone role is not.

In the first two weeks, check three things for every backup on your watch list. Is he a one-for-one backup, or are there several players who could take the role? Does he reach about 30 minutes on nights the starter sits? How healthy is the starter? If the answers are no, no and healthy, he stays on waivers.

If you drafted a backup as a flier and he has no role after the first weeks, drop him and use the bench spot for streaming. A player who needs several injuries to matter is not worth a roster spot in a league with only 2 bench slots.
